title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
screen: Film (2013, Leonardo DiCaprio); film (1974, Robert Redford)
about: A mysterious millionaire throws lavish Jazz Age parties to win back a lost love; a short, sharp take on the American Dream.

film.note: Follows the plot but swaps the novel's quiet melancholy for spectacle. The book is only 180 pages.

author: George Orwell
about: Winston Smith rebels against a surveillance state that rewrites history and polices thought. Gave us "Big Brother."

film.note: A bleak, faithful film. The book's ideas, like Newspeak and doublethink, land far better on the page.

title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
screen: BBC series (1995, Colin Firth); film (2005, Keira Knightley)
about: Witty Elizabeth Bennet and proud Mr Darcy misjudge each other in Regency England. Funnier than its reputation.

film.note: The six-hour BBC series is famously faithful. The 2005 film is lovely but condenses a lot.

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
screen: Film (2026, Margot Robbie & Jacob Elordi); film (1939); film (2011)
about: The destructive passion of Heathcliff and Cathy poisons two families on the Yorkshire moors. Nested narrators take getting used to.

film.note: Critics were split: lush and sensual, but it rewrites the story and drops the second generation.

title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
about: An orphan governess with a fierce sense of self falls for her brooding employer, who hides a terrible secret.

film.note: Well reviewed and atmospheric, but condensed. The 2006 BBC series covers more of the book.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
screen: Film (2025, Guillermo del Toro, Netflix); film (1931, Boris Karloff)
about: A scientist builds a living being, abandons it, and pays the price. More about responsibility and loneliness than horror.

film.note: Strong reviews, especially for the Creature. Keeps the novel's sympathy for him but reshapes the plot.

title: Beloved
author: Toni Morrison
about: A formerly enslaved woman is haunted, perhaps literally, by the daughter she lost. Pulitzer winner; nonlinear and intense.

film.note: Ambitious but uneven, and hard to follow without the book. Morrison's prose is the experience.

title: The Handmaid's Tale
author: Margaret Atwood
about: In a theocratic former USA, fertile women are forced to bear children for the elite. Told by one woman who remembers before.

film.note: Season 1 tracks the novel closely and won the top Emmy; later seasons invent far beyond it.

title: The Catcher in the Rye
author: J.D. Salinger
about: Expelled teenager Holden Caulfield wanders New York for a few days, raging at "phonies" and grieving more than he admits.

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
screen: Many; e.g. BBC TV film (2002, John Simm)
about: A poor student murders a pawnbroker to prove a theory and is then undone by guilt. A gripping cat-and-mouse with a detective.

film.note: A competent condensation. The novel lives inside Raskolnikov's head, which film can't reach.

title: To Kill a Mockingbird
author: Harper Lee
about: Through young Scout's eyes, her lawyer father defends a Black man falsely accused in 1930s Alabama.

film.note: One of the great adaptations; Gregory Peck won the Oscar. The book adds Scout's voice and the town.

title: The Lord of the Rings
author: J.R.R. Tolkien
about: Hobbits carry a ring of absolute power across Middle-earth to destroy it. Long, but the template for modern fantasy.

film.note: Seventeen Oscars and a superb version of the story. The book adds depth, songs and a different ending.

title: Catch-22
author: Joseph Heller
about: A WWII bombardier tries every trick to stop flying missions, trapped by absurd military logic. Very funny, then devastating.

film.note: A solid, more linear series. Much of the book's comedy is in its looping structure.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
author: Alexandre Dumas
about: A sailor betrayed and jailed for years escapes, finds a fortune and plots elaborate revenge. 1,000+ pages that fly by.

film.note: A lavish, well-reviewed three-hour French film that compresses and changes a lot. A great way in.

title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
author: Gabriel García Márquez
about: Seven generations of the Buendía family rise and fall in the mythical town of Macondo. Keep a family tree handy.

film.note: Praised as faithful and beautifully made, though some critics miss the novel's magic. Part 1 covers about half.

title: Moby-Dick
author: Herman Melville
about: Captain Ahab hunts the white whale that took his leg. Long detours into whaling and meaning; rewarding if patient.

film.note: A decent adventure film that drops the digressions, which are much of what makes the book great.

title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
about: A married aristocrat's affair destroys her place in Russian society, set against Levin's search for a meaningful life.

film.note: Stylish but stagey, and Levin's half of the novel is reduced to a sketch.

title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
about: The intertwined lives, marriages and ambitions of a provincial English town, centred on idealistic Dorothea Brooke.

film.note: A faithful, well-loved series and a good way into a long novel.

title: Lolita
author: Vladimir Nabokov
screen: Film (1962, Stanley Kubrick); film (1997, Jeremy Irons)
about: A charming, monstrous narrator tries to justify his abuse of a 12-year-old. Dazzling prose; deeply disturbing subject.

film.note: Censorship forced big changes. The novel's power is its unreliable, seductive voice.

title: Invisible Man
author: Ralph Ellison
about: A young Black man moves from the South to Harlem and finds society refuses to see him as an individual.

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
about: Orphan Pip comes into a mysterious fortune and learns hard lessons about class, gratitude and love.

film.note: A classic of British cinema. The 2023 series is darker and much looser.

title: Brave New World
author: Aldous Huxley
about: A future society keeps everyone happy through engineering, drugs and pleasure, at the cost of freedom and meaning.

film.note: Updated heavily and cancelled after one season. The 268-page book is the real thing.

title: Things Fall Apart
author: Chinua Achebe
about: Proud Igbo leader Okonkwo watches his world unravel as British missionaries and rule arrive. Short and powerful.

film.note: Hard to find and little known outside Nigeria. The book is short and powerful.

title: Slaughterhouse-Five
author: Kurt Vonnegut
about: Billy Pilgrim comes "unstuck in time" and keeps reliving the firebombing of Dresden. Dark, funny, humane.

film.note: Respected, but Vonnegut's narrating voice is the heart of the book and doesn't survive.

title: Little Women
author: Louisa May Alcott
about: The four March sisters grow up during and after the Civil War, led by aspiring writer Jo.

film.note: Greta Gerwig rearranges the timeline but keeps the spirit; widely praised.

title: Charlotte's Web
author: E.B. White
about: A clever spider saves a pig from slaughter by writing words in her web. A gentle story about friendship and death.

film.note: A beloved animated version. The book is a quick, lovely read anyway.

title: The Color Purple
author: Alice Walker
about: Celie, abused in rural Georgia, writes letters to God and slowly finds love, voice and freedom. Pulitzer winner.

film.note: Eleven Oscar nominations; it softens some of the novel's harder material.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
author: Douglas Adams
about: Seconds before Earth is demolished, Arthur Dent is rescued by an alien friend and dragged across a ridiculous universe.

film.pick: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (2005)
film.note: Fun but flat next to the book. The jokes are mostly in Adams's narration.

title: A Wrinkle in Time
author: Madeleine L'Engle
about: Meg Murry travels through space and time to rescue her scientist father from a dark force.

film.note: Visually bold but poorly reviewed, and it changes a lot. The book is a quick read.

title: The Stranger
author: Albert Camus
about: Detached Meursault kills a man on an Algerian beach and is judged more for not crying at his mother's funeral.

film.note: An elegant, well-reviewed black-and-white film that stays close. The book is only 123 pages.

title: Dune
author: Frank Herbert
screen: Films (2021 & 2024, Denis Villeneuve); film (1984, David Lynch)
about: A noble heir is thrown onto a desert planet that holds the universe's most valuable resource. Politics, ecology, religion.

film.note: Villeneuve's two films cover the novel faithfully. The book adds inner thoughts and politics.

title: The Alchemist
author: Paulo Coelho
about: A shepherd boy follows a recurring dream from Spain to the Egyptian pyramids in search of treasure and his purpose.

title: Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
screen: Many loose versions; e.g. The Man Who Killed Don Quixote (2018)
about: A man who has read too many chivalry tales sets out as a knight with his squire Sancho Panza. Often called the first modern novel.

film.pick: The Man Who Killed Don Quixote (2018)
film.note: Inspired by the book rather than an adaptation of it.

title: Ulysses
author: James Joyce
about: One ordinary day in 1904 Dublin, told through constantly shifting styles and streams of thought. The famous hardest read.

film.note: Selective and little seen. Ulysses is about its language, which film can't carry.

title: Madame Bovary
author: Gustave Flaubert
about: A doctor's wife, bored by provincial life and fed on romance novels, seeks escape through affairs and debt.

film.note: Handsome but flat. Flaubert's precise, ironic narration is the point.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
author: Lewis Carroll
screen: Disney animated film (1951); film (2010, Tim Burton)
about: Alice follows a white rabbit into a world of nonsense logic, wordplay and mad tea parties.

film.note: Blends both Alice books into a classic cartoon. The original is short and funnier.

title: Lord of the Flies
author: William Golding
about: Schoolboys stranded on an island try to govern themselves and descend into savagery.

film.note: Peter Brook's stark, faithful black-and-white version.

title: Gulliver's Travels
author: Jonathan Swift
screen: TV miniseries (1996, Ted Danson); film (2010, Jack Black)
about: A ship's surgeon visits tiny, giant and stranger peoples, each a sharp mirror of human folly.

film.note: An Emmy-winning miniseries that keeps all four voyages. Skip the 2010 comedy.

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
author: Zora Neale Hurston
about: Janie Crawford's journey through three marriages toward her own voice in early 1900s Florida. Dialogue in dialect.

film.note: A pleasant TV film. Hurston's language is the reason to read it.

title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
screen: Film (1948, Laurence Olivier); film (1996, Kenneth Branagh)
about: A prince seeks revenge for his father's murder and is paralysed by doubt. Read with notes or alongside a performance.

film.verdict: Watching is a fine way in
film.note: Uses the full text over four hours. Plays are written to be seen, so watching first is a great way in.

title: A Passage to India
author: E.M. Forster
about: A false accusation against an Indian doctor exposes the gulf between British rulers and Indians in the 1920s.

film.note: David Lean's last film, Oscar-winning and faithful to the story.

title: The Age of Innocence
author: Edith Wharton
about: A New York gentleman engaged to the perfect fiancée falls for her unconventional cousin in rigid 1870s society.

film.note: Scorsese keeps much of Wharton's narration as voiceover. One of the most faithful adaptations.

title: Fahrenheit 451
author: Ray Bradbury
about: A fireman whose job is burning books begins to read them, and to question everything.

film.note: A respected classic that changes the ending. Skip the 2018 HBO version.

title: Animal Farm
author: George Orwell
about: Farm animals overthrow their farmer, then watch the pigs become the new tyrants. The Russian Revolution in 100 pages.

film.note: The animated film changes the ending. The book is only 141 pages.

title: The Kite Runner
author: Khaled Hosseini
about: An Afghan man returns to Kabul under the Taliban to atone for betraying his childhood friend.

film.note: A respectful film. The book's guilt and inner life carry the emotion.

title: The Book Thief
author: Markus Zusak
about: Narrated by Death, a foster girl in Nazi Germany steals books and shares them with a Jewish man hidden in the basement.

film.note: Pleasant but safe. The book's narrator, Death, mostly disappears.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
about: Three brothers and the murder of their father frame Dostoevsky's great debate on faith, doubt and free will.

film.note: Hollywood melodrama. The novel is about the ideas, which the film drops.

title: The Diary of a Young Girl
author: Anne Frank
screen: Film (1959); many stage and TV versions
about: A Jewish teenager's diary from two years hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam. Ordinary, funny and heartbreaking.

film.note: An Oscar-winning film. Her own words on the page are far more powerful.

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
about: An aging English butler takes a road trip and slowly realises what his loyalty and restraint have cost him.

film.note: Anthony Hopkins and Emma Thompson; one of the finest literary adaptations.

title: Midnight's Children
author: Salman Rushdie
about: A boy born at the exact moment of India's independence finds his life magically bound to his nation's history.

film.note: Rushdie wrote the script himself, but the novel's sprawl doesn't fit in two hours.

title: Say Nothing
author: Patrick Radden Keefe
about: A mother of ten vanishes in 1972 Belfast; the search for her unlocks the whole story of the Troubles. Gripping and humane.

film.note: Widely praised; it centres the Price sisters more than the McConville investigation.

title: Nothing Is True and Everything Is Possible
author: Peter Pomerantsev
about: A TV producer's vivid, often darkly funny portrait of Putin-era Moscow, from oligarchs to models to propagandists. Short.

title: Prisoner
author: Jason Rezaian
about: The closest parallel: a Washington Post reporter held 544 days in Iran's Evin prison as a diplomatic bargaining chip.

title: Nothing to Envy
author: Barbara Demick
about: Six ordinary North Koreans from one city, followed through famine and escape. Reads like a novel; you learn a country.

title: Patriot
author: Alexei Navalny
screen: Not the book, but related: documentary Navalny (2022, Oscar winner)
about: The opposition leader's posthumous memoir, written partly from the Russian prison where he died. Warm, funny, defiant.

title: Secondhand Time
author: Svetlana Alexievich
screen: Stage versions only; her Voices from Chernobyl informed HBO's Chernobyl (2019)
about: The Nobel laureate's oral history of ordinary Russians living through the Soviet collapse. Best read in pieces; emotionally heavy.

title: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich
author: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
about: One day in a Soviet labour camp, in under 200 pages. The natural next step after Gershkovich.

film.pick: One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1970)
film.note: A faithful film, but the book is only 182 pages.

title: Long Walk to Freedom
author: Nelson Mandela
about: Mandela's life story, including 27 years in prison. Long but very readable.

film.note: Idris Elba is strong, but 27 years in prison is compressed into a few scenes.

title: Night
author: Elie Wiesel
about: A teenager's account of surviving Auschwitz. Short and unforgettable.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
about: Why our minds make predictable mistakes. Changes how you see your own decisions.

title: “Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!”
author: Richard Feynman
about: Hilarious stories from a physicist's life: safecracking, bongo drums and the atomic bomb.

title: Poor Economics
author: Abhijit Banerjee & Esther Duflo
about: How poverty actually works, told through real families and experiments.

title: I Am Malala
author: Malala Yousafzai
screen: Not the book, but related: documentary He Named Me Malala (2015)
about: The schoolgirl shot by the Taliban for wanting an education, in her own words.

title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor Frankl
about: A psychiatrist on what kept people alive in the concentration camps. Short, and one of the most influential books of its century.

title: If This Is a Man
author: Primo Levi
about: A chemist's precise, humane account of a year in Auschwitz.

title: Sapiens
author: Yuval Noah Harari
about: The whole history of humankind told as one sweeping, readable story.

title: The Emperor of All Maladies
author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
about: A Pulitzer-winning biography of cancer that reads like a novel.

film.pick: Cancer: The Emperor of All Maladies (PBS, 2015)
film.note: A well-made documentary series. The book goes much deeper into the history.

title: Pale Blue Dot
author: Carl Sagan
screen: Not the book, but related: Sagan's Cosmos TV series (1980)
about: The cosmos and humanity's place in it, beautifully written.

title: The Suitcase
author: Sergei Dovlatov
about: Eight wry, very funny stories, each built around one object Dovlatov carried out of the Soviet Union into exile in 1978. Soviet absurdity through small things.
screen: Not the book, but related: biopic Dovlatov (2018, Aleksei German Jr.)

title: A Manual for Living
author: Epictetus
about: Sharon Lebell's modern rendering of the Enchiridion, the ex-slave philosopher's short handbook: focus only on what is in your control. Read it in an evening, return to it for years.

title: Life and Fate
author: Vasily Grossman
about: The Battle of Stalingrad and the lives around it, from the front to the Gulag and the camps. Banned by the Soviets and smuggled out; often called the War and Peace of the 20th century.

film.note: A well-acted 12-part series that condenses the novel but keeps its spirit. English subtitles can be hard to find.

title: Goodbye to Berlin
author: Christopher Isherwood
about: Sketches of Berlin's landladies, nightclub singers and drifters as the Nazis rise to power, observed by a young English writer who calls himself a camera.
screen: Cabaret (1972, Bob Fosse); I Am a Camera (1955)

film.note: Eight Oscars. Based on the stage musical, it reshapes Sally Bowles and the plot; the book is quieter and sharper.

title: Plant Him and He Will Grow
author: Andrei Rubanov
about: A young 1990s Moscow banker is jailed for financial fraud and survives years in Russian prisons, based on Rubanov's own experience. Published in English as Do Time Get Time.

title: The Little Prince
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
about: A pilot stranded in the desert meets a boy from a tiny planet. A short fable about friendship, love and what grown-ups forget; written for children, mostly understood by adults.
screen: Animated film (2015, Mark Osborne); musical film (1974)

film.note: Wraps the story in a new tale about a girl and an old aviator; the stop-motion sections follow the book closely. The book takes an hour.
